kakekotoba.reading_secondary: implicit 流 association via 長/なが root, though primarily 長 'long'
kakekotoba.interaction: The word 長からむ ('will it be long?') describes both the length of the beloved's heart/affection (constancy) and, through the conventional なが root shared with 流る, evokes the flowing, unbound quality of hair/time; primarily functions as literal 'long' modifying 心, but sets up the black hair (also long, ながい) imagery that follows, linking duration of feeling with the physical length of the hair.

kakekotoba.reading_primary: みだれて (disheveled, tangled - of hair)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: みだれて (disturbed, in emotional turmoil - of heart/mind)
kakekotoba.interaction: みだれて describes simultaneously the physical disarray of the speaker's black hair upon waking and the emotional disorder/agitation of her thoughts and feelings about her lover's uncertain constancy; the tangled hair is the outward correlate of inward turmoil, both grammatically sustained through the verb.

bipartite.kami_theme: Uncertainty over whether the beloved's heart will remain constant ('long-lasting'), likened through the image of black hair
bipartite.shimo_theme: This morning the speaker's hair lies tangled and disheveled, and so too her thoughts are thrown into disorder
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku poses an abstract doubt about the durability of the lover's affection, using 'black hair' (kurokami) as the vehicle of comparison for length/constancy; the shimo-no-ku reveals that this very hair lies disheveled this morning, and the disorder of the hair becomes the visible, physical correlate of the speaker's inner emotional disarray — the poem pivots from doubt about duration to the lived sensation of turmoil, with the tangled hair standing as an implicit simile for the tangled heart.

kigo.note: Black hair (kurokami) is a staple image of court love poetry but carries no fixed seasonal association; it functions here as a symbol of youth, beauty, and the physical manifestation of emotional disorder rather than as a seasonal marker. No other lexical item in the poem (長からむ, 心, みだれて, けさ, 物思ふ) carries seasonal weight either — けさ ('this morning') is temporal but not seasonal, and 物を思ふ is a conventional expression of love-longing without seasonal specificity.
